packages.name: proc
packages.doc:
Package proc is the capability-preflight facade for the process-supervision
domain. Some proc primitives have no native, secure mechanic on every OS
(cgroup is Linux, Windows and FreeBSD only, rlimit/sd_notify are Unix-only,
the OOM bias Linux-only, …); the SDK
honours those gaps by returning the typed [UnsupportedPlatform] error and
NEVER panicking on its own. This package lets a CONSUMER instead choose to
fail fast at its own startup — the idiomatic Go MustX pattern
([regexp.MustCompile] / [text/template.Must]): the library offers the panic,
it never imposes it.

# Why preflight instead of recover

A process supervisor (a PID1) cannot rely on a recover() in its hot path: an
unrecovered panic in pid 1 orphans every supervised service, and a panic that
crosses a CGO/FFI boundary is undefined behaviour. The safe pattern is to
reject an unsupported configuration up front — assert the required
capabilities once, at startup, then route only to capabilities that
[Supported] reports present.

	func main() {
		// crash-at-launch, clearly, if this host cannot supervise at all:
		proc.MustSupport(proc.CapProcessSpawn, proc.CapReaper)
		os.Exit(run())
	}

	// elsewhere, branch instead of crash for an optional capability:
	if proc.Supported(proc.CapCgroup) {
		// confine via cgroup / Job Object
	}

# Capability × platform matrix

Every row is the engines' own answer: a capability marked ❌ is refused with
[UnsupportedPlatform] by its engine, and one marked ✅ is not, which a test of
this package holds on every platform the SDK's runtime lanes run.

	Capability           linux darwin windows freebsd openbsd netbsd dragonfly illumos solaris
	CapProcessSpawn        ✅     ✅     ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅        ✅      ✅
	CapSignalRelay         ✅     ✅     ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅        ✅      ✅
	CapReaper              ✅     ✅     ✅¹     ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅        ✅⁴     ✅⁴
	CapCgroup              ✅     ❌     ✅²     ✅²     ❌      ❌      ❌        ❌      ❌
	CapRlimit              ✅     ✅     ❌³     ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅        ✅      ✅
	CapUmaskNice           ✅     ✅     ❌      ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅        ✅      ✅
	CapOOMScoreAdj         ✅     ❌     ❌      ❌      ❌      ❌      ❌        ❌      ❌
	CapSdNotify            ✅     ✅     ❌      ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅        ✅      ✅
	CapSocketActivation    ✅     ✅     ❌      ✅      ✅      ✅      ✅        ✅      ✅
	CapDieWithParent       ✅     ❌     ✅      ✅      ❌      ❌      ❌        ❌      ❌
	CapScheduling          ✅     ❌     ❌⁵     ✅⁶     ❌      ❌      ❌        ❌      ❌
	CapPTY                 ✅     ✅     ❌      ✅      ✅      ❌      ❌        ❌      ❌
	CapProcessHandle       ✅     ❌     ✅      ❌      ❌      ❌      ❌        ❌      ❌
	CapSandbox             ✅⁷    ❌     ❌      ❌      ❌      ❌      ❌        ❌      ❌

¹ Windows has no zombies; the reaper is a correct no-op there. ² Windows
cgroup is the Job Object backend; FreeBSD's is the rctl(8) backend, which
needs a kernel carrying RACCT (kern.racct.enable=1): without it
cgroup.Available reports false and cgroup.Create returns
[UnsupportedPlatform]. ³ the Unix setrlimit-on-self model has no
Windows analogue; Windows resource limits are applied through the cgroup
(Job Object) container or at spawn via the process Spec, not a standalone rlimit.
⁴ illumos and Solaris have no reparent-here facility, like darwin, OpenBSD
and NetBSD: SetChildSubreaper returns [UnsupportedPlatform]. Their reaper
also sweeps once a second, because the Go runtime forks every child there
with FORK_NOSIGCHLD and its exit posts no SIGCHLD. Both columns are proven
on OmniOS r151054 and Oracle Solaris 11.4 (amd64) by the SDK's
cross-platform runtime lane.
⁵ Windows maps Spec.Nice onto a priority class, but has no scheduling
policy or I/O class. ⁶ FreeBSD applies SchedFIFO, SchedRR and SchedIdle
through rtprio(2); it has no batch policy and no per-process I/O class.
⁷ on amd64 and arm64, the architectures whose system call tables the sandbox's
seccomp filter is written against; Linux on any other GOARCH refuses it.

[Supported] consults runtime.GOOS only — CapSandbox's row is written for the
GOARCH the binary is built for — it is the platform-level matrix, not a runtime
probe. A capability that is native on the GOOS may still be unavailable at
runtime (e.g. cgroup present but not delegated); use the per-facade probe for
that (e.g. cgroup.Available()).

packages.name: bpf
packages.doc:
Package bpf attaches BPF programs to a control group: a device policy
(cgroup_device), an IP policy that also counts the traffic (cgroup_skb),
a bind policy (cgroup_sock_addr) — ADR 0215.

	import _ "github.com/kitsunium/sdk/third-party/ebpf/cgroup" // links the backend

	p, err := bpf.AttachDevice(tree.Path(), bpf.DevicePolicy{
		Default: bpf.Deny,
		Rules: []bpf.DeviceRule{
			{Type: bpf.DeviceChar, Major: 1, Minor: 3, Access: bpf.AccessAll, Verdict: bpf.Allow},
		},
	})

# The backend is linked by an import

Loading a BPF program takes a library the standard library does not have,
so the backend is the vendor module third-party/ebpf, over cilium/ebpf. A
program that imports github.com/kitsunium/sdk/third-party/ebpf/cgroup —
a blank import is enough — links it; any other program links nothing of
cilium/ebpf, and every call here answers [NotLinked]. Off Linux on amd64
and arm64 the backend answers [UnsupportedPlatform]; without CAP_BPF, or
on a kernel without cgroup programs, [LoadRefused]. Nothing is ever a
silent no-op. Call [Probe] once, at wiring time, to learn which.

# What is refused before anything is loaded

A policy is validated first ([PolicyInvalid], the fields naming the rule
and the field): a verdict is [Allow] or [Deny] and never the zero, the
default included, so a policy that does not say what it decides is
refused rather than read as allow-all or deny-all. The group is an
absolute directory on cgroup v2 below the hierarchy's root — what a
GroupTree's Path returns —; another one is [AttachFailed].

# Beside the other programs, and for how long

Every program is attached with BPF_F_ALLOW_MULTI: an operation passes
only when every program of the group and of its ancestors lets it
through. A program stays attached until its [Program].Close, or until the
group is removed: the supervisor may exit first, and its services stay
under their policies.

packages.name: buildinfo
packages.doc:
Package buildinfo is what the running binary was built from: the toolchain,
the main package, the main module with its version-control stamp, and every
dependency followed through its replacement.

	build, ok := buildinfo.Build()
	sdk, found := build.Module("github.com/kitsunium/sdk")
	// sdk.Version is a release ("v0.4.6"), or "" with sdk.Revision/sdk.Time
	// for a pseudo-version, or "" with sdk.Local for a directory.

A module's recorded version conflates three things, and [Module] keeps them
apart: a RELEASE in Version, a COMMIT in Revision and Time (a pseudo-version
names one, and so does the main module's version-control stamp), and a
DIRECTORY in Local and Dir (a replace, a workspace module). Nothing here fails:
a binary built without module support reads as false.

The same values are re-exported by pkg/v1/proc/process, beside the spawning of
children and the process's runtime statistics. This package is the reading
alone, so that a program asking only what it was built from imports neither
the spawn engine nor runtime/metrics, whose initialisation every process
importing them pays at start (ADR 0172).

packages.name: cgroup
packages.doc:
Package cgroup creates and manages cgroup v2 control groups to confine a
process tree's memory, CPU, pids, and IO.

It is the thin public facade over internal/service/proc/cgroup: Group is an
alias of the core proc.Group port and the functions delegate straight to the
service implementation. The kernel-enforced control-group backend is the
unified cgroup v2 hierarchy on Linux, a Job Object on Windows and rctl(8) on
FreeBSD; the facade degrades gracefully — on a platform with no such backend
(darwin, OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly, illumos, Solaris, a FreeBSD kernel
without RACCT), a cgroup
v1 host, or an unprivileged/non-delegated Linux host it returns the typed
UnsupportedPlatform or CgroupUnavailable error rather than panicking.

# Usage

Create a group, cap its memory, attach a process, then tear it down:

	import (
		"github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/cgroup"
	)

	if !cgroup.Available() {
		// cgroup v2 not mounted or not delegated to this caller.
		return
	}
	g, err := cgroup.Create("myservice")
	if err != nil {
		return // CgroupUnavailable / CgroupCreateFailed / UnsupportedPlatform
	}
	defer g.Delete()
	_ = g.SetMemoryMax(256 << 20) // 256 MiB; a negative value means "no limit"
	_ = g.SetCPUMax(50000, 100000) // 50% of one CPU ("quota period" microseconds)
	_ = g.Add(pid)                 // move pid into the group via cgroup.procs

# Semantics

Set*Max writes the matching cgroup v2 interface file: memory.max, cpu.max
("quota period"), pids.max, and one io.max line written verbatim. A negative
numeric value writes the literal "max" (no limit). Add writes a pid to
cgroup.procs. Delete rmdir's the group, which the kernel refuses (EBUSY,
surfaced as CgroupDeleteFailed) until every process has left it.

# Delegation

Available is honest about delegation: it confirms the cgroup.controllers
marker exists AND that a throwaway sub-directory can be created under the
mount. A read-only root (the common unprivileged-container case) reports
false, and Create returns CgroupUnavailable. Use WithRoot to target a
delegated sub-tree handed to the caller by a container manager.

# Platform notes

The backend is cgroup v2 on Linux, a Job Object on Windows and rctl(8) on
FreeBSD. On those, Available reports true (Linux additionally requires the
hierarchy delegated, FreeBSD a kernel with RACCT) and Create returns a usable
Group. On every other platform (darwin, OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly, illumos, Solaris) Available
returns false and Create returns UnsupportedPlatform. The Group surface is
uniform; SetIOMax / Freeze / Thaw degrade to UnsupportedPlatform on the Job
Object backend, which has no equivalent for them. WithRoot names a directory of
the cgroup v2 hierarchy, so it takes effect on Linux only: the Job Object and
rctl backends have no hierarchy, and accept the option and ignore it.

packages.name: dbus
packages.doc:
Package dbus is the SDK's message bus client, on the standard library: who
owns a well-known name on a D-Bus daemon and every change of it — what
proc/service's Type=dbus is up on — and a name a Go service owns.

	conn, err := dbus.NewConn(ctx, dbus.SystemBusAddress())
	cfg.BusWatcher = conn // proc/service: Type=dbus, BusName=
	defer conn.Close()

A service that is itself a Type=dbus unit owns its name with
RequestName once it is ready to answer on it.

# Bounds

Unix sockets only (unix:path=, unix:abstract=), AUTH EXTERNAL only, no
launched bus. A header past 64 KiB closes the connection
([CodeProtocolViolation]); a body past 1 MiB is dropped unread. A call
waits for its context ([CodeCallCancelled]); the bus's own refusal is
[CodeCallFailed], its name in the error field. Every call, and the
authentication, waits 25 seconds at most — sd-bus's default reply timeout
— or its context's deadline when sooner ([CodeCallTimeout]). Linux only:
NewConn is UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM elsewhere.

packages.name: ipc
packages.doc:
Package ipc is a private socket between processes of one machine — a
daemon and the short-lived clients that talk to it, a product and the tool
that attaches to it (ADR 0148).

	cfg := ipc.Config{Path: filepath.Join(ipc.RuntimeDir("statusline"), "daemon.sock")}
	ln, err := ipc.Listen(cfg)          // the daemon
	c, err := ipc.Dial(ctx, cfg)        // a client; c.Peer says who listens

# Who can connect

Two gates, and the package says which one holds where:

  - The DIRECTORY, everywhere. The socket lives in a directory its account
    owns and nobody else may write to — created 0700 when missing, refused
    otherwise ([CodeDirectoryUnsafe]) — and the socket file is 0600.
    Connecting needs search permission on the directory, so only its owner
    (and root) get through. The accounts Config.AllowUIDs / AllowGIDs name
    get the socket opened to them — 0660 and the group for one group,
    0666 for another user or several groups —, the directory, which the
    deployment opens to them, staying the first gate. On Windows the endpoint is a named pipe named
    after this account and the path, whose own DACL grants this account
    only, which refuses remote clients and which nobody can join once it
    exists; a name another account took first is refused as squatted
    ([CodeEndpointSquatted]), never mistaken for a daemon of ours.
  - The PEER'S CREDENTIALS, where the kernel gives them: on Linux,
    SO_PEERCRED names the peer's user, group and process, and a peer that is
    neither this account nor in Config.AllowUIDs / AllowGIDs — by its
    user, its effective group or a supplementary group the kernel
    recorded — is closed before Accept returns it — and so, since #1093,
    do FreeBSD, DragonFly and NetBSD (the effective group alone there),
    where an unnamed peer is refused too. On Windows each end
    reads the other's account from its process token ([Peer].SID) and
    refuses another one. On darwin, OpenBSD, illumos and Solaris
    [Peer].Verified is false and the directory is the only gate.

# The path to the directory is part of the gate

Every lookup — the directory's creation, the bind, the connect — follows a
link planted at a PARENT of the directory, so on Unix Listen and Dial walk
the whole path one component at a time and judge each by the directory
holding it, where ANYBODY can write that directory: a link there could have
been planted by anyone, a component another account owns could have been
created by anyone, and without the sticky bit anyone can replace what is
there. Each is refused ([CodePathUnsafe]) before anything is created or a
byte is sent. The links an operating system ships — /tmp and /var on macOS,
/var/run on Linux — live in directories only root writes and are accepted.
A socket placed under a tree another account owns trusts that account:
[RuntimeDir] places it under this account's own.

# Nothing is taken over

Listen dials a socket already at the path first. One that answers is left
alone and refused ([CodeInUse]), and so is one whose owner is alive but
busy — its accept queue full, or the dial out of time; only one the kernel
says nobody listens on — what a killed daemon leaves — is removed and
replaced, provided it IS a socket this account
owns. A client refuses a socket file another account owns
([CodeEndpointForeign]) before it sends a byte: a request never reaches an
impostor.

# Where

[RuntimeDir] names an application's directory: $RUNTIME_DIRECTORY
(systemd's, its first entry when it lists several), $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/<app>, %LOCALAPPDATA%\<app> on Windows, else
<tmp>/<app>-<uid>. [RuntimeDirOr] ends the same chain on a directory the
caller names instead of <tmp> (ADR 0182). A path is at most the shortest
sun_path any supported kernel has, less its NUL.

# Ports, and the doubles they admit

[Listener] and [Dialer] are interfaces, as net.Listener is: [Listen] and
[NewDialer] return the socket engine behind them, and code that holds one
can be handed a double in a test — connections from net.Pipe, with the
[Peer] the test chooses — instead of a socket on disk. Both are frozen at
the methods they have; a capability added later is a second interface an
endpoint may also implement, never a method added to these.

packages.name: rpc
packages.doc:
Package rpc is a call between two processes of one machine over the private
socket of proc/ipc (ADR 0218): a request and its reply, or a request and the
items a server pushes, framed, bounded and encoded in a codec format both
ends agreed on.

	srv, err := rpc.NewServer(rpc.ServerConfig{
		Formats: []codec.Format{"json"}, MaxFrameBytes: 1 << 20,
		MaxInFlight: 64, FrameTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
	}, rpc.Methods{"status": rpc.HandlerFunc(status)})
	go srv.Serve(ln) // ln from ipc.Listen

	c, err := rpc.NewClient(ctx, dialer, rpc.ClientConfig{
		Format: "json", MaxFrameBytes: 1 << 20, MaxInFlight: 64,
		FrameTimeout: 5 * time.Second, CallTimeout: 2 * time.Second,
	})
	err = c.Call(ctx, "status", req, &resp)

A format is a codec registered under its name: import the codec's package
(pkg/v1/data/codec/json, say) for it to be there.

# Bounds, every one the caller's

A frame longer than MaxFrameBytes is refused on its length, before a byte of
its body is read or allocated ([CodeFrameTooLarge]); one not whole within
FrameTimeout of its first byte closes the connection. At most MaxInFlight
calls run per connection, the next answered [CodeOverloaded] at once. A call
carries its deadline to the server, which ends the handler's context on it;
a caller that gives up sends a cancel frame ([CodeCallTimeout],
[CodeCallCancelled]). None of these bounds has a default: zero is refused
([CodeMisconfigured]).

# Errors across the socket

A handler's error carrying an SDK code reaches the caller with that code,
reason and public text, so errs.HasCode works on both sides; any other error
is [CodeRemoteFailed] there, its text kept on the server.

packages.name: memlimit
packages.doc:
Package memlimit derives the Go runtime soft memory limit from the control
group allowance governing this process, and installs it.

GOMAXPROCS has been cgroup-aware since Go 1.25; the memory limit never was. A
process in a 512 MiB container grows its heap past the cap and is SIGKILLed by
the kernel instead of being pushed into a more aggressive GC cycle. One call at
start-up converts that kill into collector pressure.

It is the thin public facade over internal/service/proc/memlimit: the types are
aliases of the core proc value types and the function delegates straight to the
service implementation.

# Usage

Apply it once, as early as possible, before the heap has grown:

	import (
		"github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/memlimit"
	)

	func main() {
		applied := memlimit.Apply()
		if applied.Applied() {
			// applied.Limit bytes, derived from applied.Allowance.
		}
	}

Apply never fails and never panics: every outcome is a value. A caller that
only wants to know whether it acted reads Applied; one that wants to log WHY it
did not reads Source, which distinguishes an operator-set GOMEMLIMIT from an
uncapped host from a cap too tight to honour.

# What the limit covers

The limit is SOFT and covers all memory mapped, managed and not released by the
Go runtime — the heap, goroutine stacks, runtime metadata. It excludes memory
the runtime does not manage: the binary image, C allocations, syscall.Mmap
mappings, and kernel memory held on the process's behalf. Subprocesses are
outside it entirely. Ninety percent of the cgroup allowance is handed to the
runtime and the remainder covers those, so this reduces OOM pressure rather
than eliminating it.

# Which cap is the allowance

The tightest on the way up. On cgroup v2 the allowance is the minimum of
memory.max and memory.high over the process's own cgroup and every ancestor:
the kernel reclaims and slows a group above memory.high long before memory.max
kills it, so the throttle is the working cap. The result's Bound says which of
the two file kinds set it (MemoryBoundHigh or MemoryBoundMax). cgroup v1 has no
such file — memory.soft_limit_in_bytes is a reclaim hint — and
memory.limit_in_bytes alone binds there.

# Relation to cgroup and rlimit

The three are distinct directions on one subject. cgroup WRITES a control group
to bound a child process. rlimit applies a setrlimit(2) ceiling the kernel
enforces by failing allocations. memlimit READS the cgroup cap already bounding
THIS process and tunes the Go collector to live inside it — nothing is enforced,
the collector simply works harder as the heap approaches the limit.

# Platform notes

Control groups are a Linux facility. Off Linux no limit file is readable, so
Apply reports MemorySourceUnconstrained and leaves the runtime default in
place; no call fails and no build tag is needed.

packages.name: process
packages.doc:
Package process is the public facade for the SDK's keystone process-spawn
primitive: it starts a child process under explicit credentials, in its own
process group and session, and returns a handle that can wait for exit, signal
the leader or its whole group, and stop the group gracefully with a
SIGTERM→SIGKILL escalation.

It is a thin facade over internal/service/proc/exec. The public types are
aliases of the internal/core/proc port, so a value built here is the same type
the service layer consumes — no conversion, no parallel hierarchy.

# Spec → systemd directive mapping

	Spec.Path / Args / Dir / Env   ExecStart= / WorkingDirectory= / Environment=
	Spec.User / Group / Groups     User= / Group= / SupplementaryGroups=
	Spec.Setpgid                   KillMode=control-group (group-killable tree)
	Spec.Setsid                    a new session, detached from the parent tty
	Spec.Nice                      Nice=
	Spec.OOMScoreAdj               OOMScoreAdjust=
	Spec.Umask                     UMask=        (applied via trampoline)
	Spec.Rlimits                   Limit*=       (applied via trampoline)

# Environment, and finding the executable

A nil Spec.Env yields an empty environment — the child never silently inherits
the supervisor's, so a spawned service starts from a known state. Pass an
explicit slice (including os.Environ()) to inherit deliberately. A key that
begins __KITSUNIUM_SDK_PROC_, in any case, belongs to the SDK's own spawn
protocol: Start refuses it with ReservedEnv before any fork.

Spec.Path may be a bare name. "go" is searched in the PATH the CHILD will
see — the PATH entry of Spec.Env whenever it names one, even empty, the
parent's only when it names none —
with os/exec's rules: the first executable in PATH order wins, and a match
found only through a relative entry ("." or an empty one) is refused with
exec.ErrDot, which the returned SpawnFailed wraps (errors.Is answers). A path
with a separator is taken as written.

# Standard streams

Spec.Stdio selects how the child's stdin/stdout/stderr are wired:
StdioInherit (the default) shares the parent's streams; StdioNull discards the
child's output and gives it an immediate-EOF stdin; StdioCapture connects
Spec.Stdout and Spec.Stderr (any io.Writer) and Spec.Stdin (any io.Reader),
with a nil stream falling back to the null device for that one stream. In
capture mode every byte the child writes reaches the writers before Wait
returns, and the copier goroutines terminate at EOF (no leak). It composes
with Setpgid/Setsid and credential drop. Stdin should be EOF-terminating.

# Stopping a process group

Stop sends the chosen signal to the entire process group, waits up to grace
for exit, then escalates to SIGKILL on the group. Because the child leads its
own group (Spec.Setpgid), forked grandchildren are reached too — no survivor
is left behind.

# Example

	spec := process.Spec{
		Path:    "/bin/sh",
		Args:    []string{"sh", "-c", "sleep 1000 & wait"},
		Setpgid: true,
	}
	p, err := process.Start(context.Background(), spec)
	if err != nil {
		// err carries a central proc sentinel code (errs.HasCode).
		return err
	}
	// Graceful stop: SIGTERM to the group, escalate to SIGKILL after 5s.
	if err := p.Stop(context.Background(), 5*time.Second, process.SIGTERM); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	exit, err := p.Wait()
	_ = exit // exit.Code / exit.Signal / exit.UserTime / exit.MaxRSS

# Resource limits and umask

The Go runtime exposes no hook to run setrlimit(2) or umask(2) in the child
between fork and exec, so Start honours Spec.Rlimits and Spec.Umask via a
re-exec trampoline: when either is set, Start spawns this binary as a tiny
self-trampoline that applies the limits in the fresh child, then execs the real
target — so the target starts already under its limits, with no cgo and no
dependency. An Rlimit naming a resource with no RLIMIT_* mapping on the platform
(NPROC, MEMLOCK — absent from stdlib syscall) is still rejected up front with
UnknownResource; a limit the kernel refuses to set (e.g. raising a hard cap
unprivileged) fails the spawn rather than running the child unconfined. Nice and
OOMScoreAdj are applied post-start on the live pid and surface a typed error if
the host refuses.

# Platforms

Unix gets everything above. Windows spawns too, through CreateProcess: stdio
wiring, Setpgid (a new console process group), Spec.Rlimits (enforced by a
Job Object) and the PATH search (with PATHEXT) all work, while the fields
with no Windows meaning at this layer — User/Group/Groups, Umask, Nice,
OOMScoreAdj, ExtraFiles, CgroupPath — are refused with UnsupportedPlatform
rather than dropped. There, SignalGroup sends a Setpgid child's group
CTRL_BREAK, which a Go child reads as os.Interrupt, and reaches the leader
alone otherwise; Stop's escalation is TerminateProcess. Every other platform returns
UnsupportedPlatform from Start; the package compiles everywhere.

# The process itself

Everything above acts on a child. [Self] and [Build] read the process they
run in, on every platform, and never fail:

	stats := process.Self()
	stats.Goroutines, stats.HeapBytes, stats.GCPauses.Quantile(0.99), stats.CPUTime

	build, ok := process.Build()
	sdk, found := build.Module("github.com/kitsunium/sdk")
	// sdk.Version is a release ("v0.4.6"), or "" with sdk.Revision/sdk.Time
	// for a pseudo-version, or "" with sdk.Local for a directory.

CPUTime is the kernel's count (getrusage, GetProcessTimes on Windows) where
the platform has one and the Go runtime's estimate elsewhere — refreshed
only at a garbage collection; Stats.CPUEstimated says which. The
distributions and every counter are cumulative since the process started —
subtract two snapshots for a window.

A module's recorded version conflates three things, and [Module] keeps them
apart: a RELEASE in Version, a COMMIT in Revision and Time (a pseudo-version
names one, and so does the main module's version-control stamp), and a
DIRECTORY in Local and Dir (a replace, a workspace module). What is in a
local directory NOW is a question for the framework's git.Head (ADR 0158).

Package process — the running process itself: what it was built from and
what it is doing.

Package process — ergonomic re-exports: the handful of signal constants and
resource sentinels callers need to drive Stop/SignalGroup and read typed
errors without importing internal/core/proc directly.

Package process — StdioMode re-exports for wiring a child's standard streams.

packages.name: reaper
packages.doc:
Package reaper is the PID1 / subreaper zombie-collector facade.

A process that becomes the parent of orphaned descendants — an init (pid 1)
in a container, or any supervisor that calls [SetChildSubreaper] — must reap
the children that reparent to it, or they accumulate as zombies that exhaust
the system's pid space. This package wraps the kernel mechanics (a SIGCHLD
handler driving a non-blocking waitpid loop, plus prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER))
behind a tiny, portable surface.

	r := reaper.New()
	r.Start()          // background: reap children as they exit
	defer r.Stop()     // final drain; no zombie outlives shutdown

	// A non-init supervisor opts in to collecting orphaned grandchildren:
	if !reaper.IsPID1() {
		if err := reaper.SetChildSubreaper(); err != nil {
			// degrade: orphans will reparent to pid 1 instead
		}
	}

# Semantics

[Reaper].Start installs an [os/signal] SIGCHLD handler and, on each signal,
loops syscall.Wait4 with WNOHANG until it drains every reapable child. Start is
idempotent. [Reaper].Stop performs one final drain and waits for the loop's
goroutine to exit, so a Start/Stop cycle leaks neither zombies nor goroutines
and may be repeated. [Reaper].ReapOnce runs a single non-blocking sweep and is
safe to call concurrently with the loop — each child's exit is observed
exactly once across whoever sweeps.

# Children spawned through pkg/v1/proc/process

A sweep collects EVERY exited child, including one a
[github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/process.Process] is waiting for. Its exit
status is not lost: the sweep hands it to that Process, whose Wait reports
the child's own exit code whichever of the two collected it. A child spawned
any other way — os/exec, syscall.ForkExec, a C library — has no such claim, so
a running reaper still takes its status and its own wait fails with ECHILD.
Spawn what you wait for through pkg/v1/proc/process in a process that runs the
reaper.

ECHILD ("no children") is treated as a clean end of a sweep, not an error; any
other wait error surfaces as the typed sentinel [ReapFailed].

# Platform notes

The real implementation is Unix-only. On platforms without SIGCHLD/waitpid
(e.g. Windows), [New] returns a no-op reaper (Start/Stop do nothing, ReapOnce
returns 0) and [SetChildSubreaper] returns [UnsupportedPlatform]. On illumos
and Solaris the Go runtime forks every child with FORK_NOSIGCHLD, so the exit
of a child this process spawned posts no SIGCHLD there; the loop also sweeps
once a second on those two, which keeps "reap children as they exit" true. Code that
links this package therefore builds and runs everywhere; only the behaviour
degrades. [SetChildSubreaper] requires no privilege but is a per-process
Linux capability; where the prctl is unavailable it returns a typed error
rather than panicking.

packages.name: rlimit
packages.doc:
Package rlimit applies per-process resource ceilings via setrlimit(2) /
prlimit64(2).

It is the thin public facade over internal/service/proc/rlimit: the types are
aliases of the core proc value types and the functions delegate straight to
the service implementation. Resources are named abstractly (Resource) and
mapped to the platform RLIMIT_* constant inside the service layer, so calling
code stays portable; on a non-Linux host every call returns the typed
UnsupportedPlatform error rather than acting.

# Usage

Lower the open-file ceiling of the current process to 1024 soft / 4096 hard:

	import (
		"github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/rlimit"
	)

	err := rlimit.Apply(0, map[rlimit.Resource]rlimit.Limit{
		rlimit.ResourceNoFile: {Soft: 1024, Hard: 4096},
	})
	if err != nil {
		// inspect with errs.HasCode(err, ...) — RlimitFailed / UnknownResource.
	}

A pid of 0 targets the calling process via setrlimit(2). Any other pid targets
that process via prlimit64(2), which requires the CAP_SYS_RESOURCE capability;
without it the call returns RlimitFailed wrapping EPERM.

# Spec integration

Go's os/exec SysProcAttr carries no rlimit field. process.Start applies a
Spec.Rlimits set to the child it spawns via a re-exec trampoline; this package
is the standalone primitive for the other cases: apply limits from the child
after fork (a pid-0 Apply in the child) or, when supervising, apply them to the
spawned pid via prlimit64. PrepareSysProcAttr validates a limit set without any
syscall — call it at Spec-construction time to fail fast on a Resource this
platform cannot honour, before a process is ever spawned.

# Platform notes

Only Linux is supported. RLIMIT_NPROC and RLIMIT_MEMLOCK are absent from Go's
syscall package and are restated from the kernel generic ABI inside the
service layer. Off Linux, Apply and PrepareSysProcAttr return
UnsupportedPlatform.

packages.name: service
packages.doc:
Package service runs one service the way systemd.service(5) does (ADR 0214):
Type=, the Exec*= commands and their prefixes, the timeouts, the watchdog,
Restart= and the start limiter, as typed values in a Config, driven by one
actor per unit over a pure reducer.

	start, _ := service.ParseCommand([]string{"/usr/bin/daemon", "--foreground"})
	unit, err := service.NewUnit(&service.Config{
		Name:      "daemon",
		ExecStart: []service.Command{start},
		Restart:   service.RestartOnFailure,
	})
	err = unit.Start(ctx)      // up, or START_FAILED with its result
	events, cancel := unit.Subscribe(0) // every change, never waited on
	err = unit.Stop(ctx)        // ExecStop=, the signals, ExecStopPost=

# Directives are values

Config holds one typed field per directive; a field's zero is systemd's
default, and Zero and Infinity are systemd's literal 0 and infinity. The
unit-file syntax, the % specifiers, the graph between units and the
actions on the system (SuccessAction=, StartLimitAction=) are the
caller's. ParseCommand reads the prefixes "@-:+!|"; "+" and "!" run only
where Config.AllowPrivilegedControl allows them.

# Observing a unit

Unit.State is the level — state, step, result, processes, a generation
that grows with every change. Unit.Subscribe's queue is bounded and the
unit never waits on it: the newest event is dropped when it is full,
counted, and a consumer that sees a gap in the generations reads
Unit.State.

# A daemon that forks

Type=forking adopts the daemon its command leaves through an Attacher —
NewAttacher's, on Linux, darwin and the BSDs: the PID PIDFile= names, or,
on Linux, with a Cgroup that lists its members (CgroupMembers), the one
member whose parent is outside the cgroup (GuessMainPID=).

# The descriptor store

FileDescriptorStoreMax= keeps the descriptors a service hands with
FDSTORE=1 and gives them back to its next main process, at fd 3 on with
their FDNAME=; Unit.FDStore lists them. Linux only.

# One instance per connection

SpawnInstance runs a unit of a template for one accepted connection —
Accept=yes —, the connection at fd 3 (LISTEN_FDS=1), ended with its run.
Not on Windows.

# The unit's control group

A Cgroup that is a CgroupUnit — proc/cgroup's group, on Linux — runs
KillMode=control-group (then the default) and mixed, ExitType=cgroup,
Delegate= and OOMPolicy=, every process of the unit spawned into it.
NewAttacher's scope names a cgroup as /proc/<pid>/cgroup does:
proc/cgroup's Membership turns a group's directory into that path.

# Type=dbus

A Type=dbus unit is up once its main process runs and its BusName= is
owned — its Config.BusWatcher, pkg/v1/proc/dbus's Conn, follows the
name —, and stops when the bus announces the name lost. Linux only.

# The sandbox

ProtectSystem=, PrivateTmp=, ReadOnlyPaths=, BindPaths=,
TemporaryFileSystem=, RootDirectory=, the Private…= namespaces,
ProtectHostname=, NoNewPrivileges=, the capability sets, SecureBits= and
SystemCallFilter= are Config fields, resolved into proc/process's
Sandbox on Linux amd64 and arm64 — refused elsewhere —, added to the one
Config.Spec carries. A "+" command runs unconfined, a "!" one keeps the
sandbox; a start whose sandbox cannot be applied is START_FAILED
wrapping SANDBOX_FAILED or SANDBOX_UNAVAILABLE.

# Platforms

The reducer and every type that needs no notification run everywhere.
Notifications need a NotifySource — ListenNotify on Linux and FreeBSD.
Windows kills and does nothing else: a signal other than SIGKILL is
refused there.

packages.name: signal
packages.doc:
Package signal is the typed signal toolbox: parse, subscribe, and forward OS
signals through one ergonomic surface.

It is a thin facade over the SDK process-supervision domain. Signals are typed
values ([Signal]) that round-trip through their canonical name, [Notify]
subscribes to a set of them on a leak-free channel, and [Relay] forwards a
stream of received signals to another process or process group.

	// Translate a graceful-shutdown request and act on it.
	term, _ := signal.Parse("SIGTERM")         // typed value
	intr, _ := signal.Parse("SIGINT")
	ch, stop := signal.Notify(term, intr)
	defer stop()                               // leak-free teardown
	<-ch                                       // block until a signal arrives

	// Forward every signal we receive down to a child process group.
	src, stop := signal.Notify(term)
	defer stop()
	go signal.Relay(src, signal.Target(-childPGID)) // negative ⇒ process group

# Notify semantics

[Notify] registers an os/signal subscription and runs a translation goroutine
that converts each delivery to a typed [Signal]. The returned channel is
buffered (one slot per subscribed signal, floor of one) so a burst is not
dropped while the reader is busy. The returned stop function detaches the
subscription, ends the goroutine, and closes the channel; it is idempotent and
leaves no goroutine or registration behind.

# Relay semantics

[Relay] reads from the source channel and delivers each signal to the
[Target] — via kill(2) on Unix. A positive [Target] is a pid; a [Target] below
-1 addresses the process group whose id is its absolute value. Relay returns
when the source channel closes (nil) or when a delivery fails (a typed
RELAY_FAILED error). The reserved targets 0 and -1 are refused on every
platform before anything is delivered.

# Platform notes

Parse, String, and Notify are portable. Relay has a native backend on Unix
(kill(2)) and on Windows, which has no kill(2): a pid target is terminated
with TerminateProcess, and a process-group target receives a console control
event: CTRL_BREAK, SIGINT included, since Windows delivers no CTRL_C to one
group. On the remaining platforms it
returns the typed UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM sentinel rather than acting, so code
compiles and degrades gracefully everywhere.

packages.name: listen
packages.doc:
Package listen is the public facade for systemd-style socket activation
(sd_listen_fds(3)): a service recovers already-bound listening sockets handed
to it by an activator, and an activator hands sockets to a child it spawns.

It is the symmetric companion to pkg/v1/proc/systemd/notify (readiness) and is generic to
any networked program: zero-downtime restarts, on-demand start, and inetd-style
launching all rest on passing a bound socket to a fresh process so no
connection is lost and no bind races.

# Service side

A socket-activated process recovers its inherited listeners:

	lns, err := listen.Listeners(true) // unsetEnv: true so children don't re-inherit
	if err != nil {
		return err // UnsupportedPlatform off Unix; LISTEN_FAILED on a bad fd
	}
	for _, ln := range lns {
		go serve(ln)
	}

Files returns the raw *os.File sockets, Listeners wraps the stream sockets as
net.Listener, and WithNames groups them by their LISTEN_FDNAMES name (duplicate
names allowed). All honour LISTEN_PID: fds addressed to a different process are
ignored (an empty result, not an error).

# Activator side

Prepare is the symmetric half — it makes the protocol self-contained and
testable without systemd. It appends each listener's socket to the child Spec's
inherited files and sets LISTEN_FDS / LISTEN_FDNAMES so the child recovers them:

	ln, _ := net.Listen("tcp", ":8080")
	spec := process.Spec{Path: "/usr/bin/myservice"}
	if err := listen.Prepare(&spec, map[string]net.Listener{"http": ln}); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	p, err := process.Start(ctx, spec) // the child finds the socket at fd 3

LISTEN_PID is intentionally omitted by Prepare: a pre-fork activator cannot know
the child's pid, so the receiving side accepts an absent LISTEN_PID from a
trusted parent while still validating a present one (the systemd-set case).

# Platform

Socket activation relies on Unix file-descriptor inheritance. Off Unix every
function returns the typed UnsupportedPlatform sentinel; the package compiles
on every GOOS.

GroupWatcher is the Linux sibling of a Group that follows cgroup.events and
memory.events: Watch. It aliases the core port.

symbols.name: IOStat
symbols.doc: IOStat is one device's I/O by a group. It aliases the core value.

symbols.name: JobLimiter
symbols.doc:
JobLimiter is the Windows sibling of a Group that caps the memory of the
whole Job Object, where SetMemoryMax caps each process: SetJobMemoryLimit.
It aliases the core port.

symbols.name: Membership
symbols.doc:
Membership returns the path /proc/<pid>/cgroup names for a process of the
group whose directory is dir — what process.AttachScope's Cgroup takes —:
"/sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/web.service" is "/system.slice/web.service".
A group's Path is that directory, never this path. InvalidSpec when no
cgroup2 mount holds dir; UnsupportedPlatform off Linux.

symbols.name: MemoryEvents
symbols.doc: MemoryEvents counts what a group's memory limits did. It aliases the core value.

symbols.name: MustCreate
symbols.doc:
MustCreate is like [Create] but panics with the typed error when creation
fails — UnsupportedPlatform on a platform with no control-group backend
(darwin, OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly, illumos, Solaris), or CgroupUnavailable when the Linux hierarchy is not
delegated. It is the idiomatic Go MustX opt-in (like
[regexp.MustCompile]) for a consumer that chooses crash-on-unsupported at its
own startup; the SDK itself never panics, and [Create] is the non-panicking
form for normal use. The panic value is the typed error, so a top-level
recover() can classify it via errs.CodeOf / HasCode.

symbols.name: Option
symbols.doc:
Option customises a Create call (functional-option pattern). It aliases the
service Option type; construct options with WithRoot.

symbols.name: Probe
symbols.doc:
Probe reports what the caller may do under a control-group root — WithRoot's,
else the mount — where Available answers for the mount root alone. On a
host that delegates a subtree, Probe(WithRoot(p.OwnGroup)) is the gate
Create can be used behind. UnsupportedPlatform where no backend exists.

symbols.name: ProbeResult
symbols.doc:
ProbeResult is what Probe found under a control-group root: whether it is
mounted, whether the caller may create a group there, its controllers,
and the caller's own cgroup. It aliases the service value.

symbols.name: WithControllers
symbols.doc:
WithControllers enables ctrls for the group Create makes, on Linux: they
are written to the cgroup.subtree_control of the root and of every group
down to the new one before it is made, so its interface files for them
exist. A controller the root does not offer is CgroupControllerAbsent
before anything is made. Windows and FreeBSD accept it and ignore it.

symbols.name: WithRoot
symbols.doc:
WithRoot overrides the parent directory under which Create makes the new
control group, targeting a delegated sub-tree instead of the top-level mount.
It is a cgroup v2 path: on Windows and FreeBSD, whose backends have no
hierarchy, it is accepted and ignored.

symbols.name: Config
symbols.doc:
Config is where a private socket lives and who, besides its own
account, may use it — the engine's configuration, shared by both ends.

symbols.name: Conn
symbols.doc: Conn is a connection with its peer's identity.

symbols.name: Dial
symbols.doc: Dial connects to the private socket at cfg.Path, within ctx and one second.

symbols.name: Dialer
symbols.doc:
Dialer is the connecting end of a private socket: it reaches the
listener its configuration names, and refuses one it cannot trust
before a byte is sent.

symbols.name: FileReceiver
symbols.doc:
FileReceiver receives the files a FileSender passed, at most max per
message, the excess closed — by the kernel on Unix, in the sender on
Windows; assert it on Conn.Conn.

symbols.name: FileSender
symbols.doc:
FileSender passes open files to the peer's process (SCM_RIGHTS on Unix;
DuplicateHandle on Windows, WSADuplicateSocketW for a socket, a TCP
listener's file among them); assert it on Conn.Conn. Only to a peer the
kernel named.

symbols.name: Listen
symbols.doc:
Listen opens the private socket at cfg.Path and returns the engine behind
the Listener port.

symbols.name: Listener
symbols.doc:
Listener is the accepting end of a private socket: it hands out the
connections of admitted peers only, and closes and counts the others.

symbols.name: NewDialer
symbols.doc:
NewDialer returns the engine behind the Dialer port for the private socket
at cfg.Path. The configuration is checked here, before anything is touched,
and copied: editing cfg's slices afterwards changes nothing.

symbols.name: Peer

symbols.name: Apply
symbols.doc:
Apply derives the Go soft memory limit from the tightest control-group cap
governing this process and installs it, returning what it read, what it
derived, and what decided the outcome.

It stands aside — leaving the runtime default in place — when GOMEMLIMIT is
already set, when no cgroup declares a cap, and when the derived limit is too
small to be useful. Those three are told apart by Limit.Source.

symbols.name: ApplyWith
symbols.doc:
ApplyWith is Apply with the caller's Config. It returns an error carrying
MEMLIMIT_MISCONFIGURED, and installs nothing, for a headroom outside (0, 100]
percent or a negative floor.

symbols.name: Bound
symbols.doc:
Bound names the control-group file that set a derivation's allowance. It
aliases the core proc type.

symbols.name: Config
symbols.doc:
Config tunes a derivation: the share of the allowance handed to the runtime,
the floor, and the GC percent installed with the limit. Its zero value is
Apply's. It aliases the service value.

symbols.name: Limit
symbols.doc:
Limit is an immutable record of one derivation: the allowance read, the limit
derived, and the source that decided it. It aliases the core proc type.

symbols.name: MemoryBoundHigh
symbols.doc:
MemoryBoundHigh reports that a memory.high file — the kernel's throttle —
bound the derivation. It re-exports the core enum value.

symbols.name: MemoryBoundMax
symbols.doc:
MemoryBoundMax reports that the hard cap — memory.max, or cgroup v1's
memory.limit_in_bytes — bound the derivation. It re-exports the core enum
value.

symbols.name: MemorySourceBelowFloor
symbols.doc:
MemorySourceBelowFloor reports that a cap was found but the limit derived from
it fell under the usable floor and was discarded.

symbols.name: MemorySourceCgroup
symbols.doc:
MemorySourceCgroup reports the one outcome that yields a limit: a real cap was
read from the control-group hierarchy and the derived value was applied.

symbols.name: MemorySourceOperator
symbols.doc:
MemorySourceOperator reports that GOMEMLIMIT carried a non-empty value, which
the runtime has already applied. It re-exports the core enum value so consumers
qualify it as memlimit.MemorySourceOperator.

symbols.name: MemorySourceUnconstrained
symbols.doc:
MemorySourceUnconstrained reports that no control group governing this process
declares a memory cap.

symbols.name: Source
symbols.doc: Source names what decided the soft memory limit. It aliases the core proc type.

symbols.name: Watch
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, clk clock.Timed, every time.Duration, cfg Config, onChange func(Limit)) error
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, clk github.com/kitsunium/sdk/internal/kernel/clock.Timed, every time.Duration, cfg github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/memlimit.Config, onChange func(github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/memlimit.Limit)) error
symbols.doc:
Watch applies the limit as ApplyWith does, then re-derives it every period on
clk until ctx ends, installing and reporting it again only when it changed —
a resize of the control group under the running process. A period under a
second is clamped to a second; a lifted cap puts the runtime's default back.
It blocks until ctx ends.

symbols.name: AdoptionRefused

code.public: The process may not be adopted

symbols.doc:
AdoptionRefused is returned by Attach and AttachPIDFile for a process they
may not adopt.

symbols.name: Attach
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, pid int) (proc Process, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, pid int) (proc github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/process.Process, err error)
symbols.doc:
Attach adopts a running process this one did not spawn, held through a pidfd
on Linux and kqueue knotes on darwin and the BSDs: its Wait returns once the
process has ended, with StatusUnknown — only a parent reads an exit status.
PID 1 and this process are AdoptionRefused; illumos, Solaris and Windows
return UnsupportedPlatform.

symbols.name: AttachPIDFile
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, path string, want AttachScope) (proc Process, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, path string, want github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/process.AttachScope) (proc github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/process.Process, err error)
symbols.doc:
AttachPIDFile reads the PID file at path safely — absolute, walked without a
symbolic link at its end, a regular file holding one PID, else
PIDFileRefused — and adopts the process it names as Attach does. A file
another user could have written or redirected is trusted only through want:
the process must lie in its cgroup and run as one of its users, and a want
that bounds nothing is AdoptionRefused. Linux, darwin and the BSDs; off Linux
a cgroup bound is AdoptionRefused, as there is no cgroup to check.

symbols.name: AttachScope
symbols.doc:
AttachScope bounds the process an untrustworthy PID file may name: a cgroup
v2 subtree and the users it may run as. It is an alias of the core port's
AttachValue.

symbols.doc:

symbols.name: EnvDeny

symbols.doc:
Identity is what the kernel says the running process is: its start, the
digest and build id of its binary, its container, pid namespace and boot.
It is an alias of the service value.

symbols.name: Landlock
symbols.doc:
Landlock restricts a sandboxed child's filesystem access. It is an alias of the
core port's LandlockValue.

symbols.name: LandlockABI
symbols.doc:
LandlockABI returns the Landlock ABI version the running kernel implements;
a Landlock right newer than it is refused unless named best-effort.
SandboxUnavailable without Landlock, UnsupportedPlatform off Linux amd64 and
arm64.

symbols.name: LandlockAccess
symbols.doc:
LandlockAccess is a set of Landlock filesystem rights. It is an alias of the
core port type.

symbols.name: LandlockExecute
symbols.doc: LandlockExecute is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_EXECUTE (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockIoctlDev
symbols.doc: LandlockIoctlDev is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_IOCTL_DEV (ABI 5, Linux 6.10).

symbols.name: LandlockMakeBlock
symbols.doc: LandlockMakeBlock is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_MAKE_BLOCK (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockMakeChar
symbols.doc: LandlockMakeChar is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_MAKE_CHAR (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockMakeDir
symbols.doc: LandlockMakeDir is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_MAKE_DIR (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockMakeFifo
symbols.doc: LandlockMakeFifo is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_MAKE_FIFO (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockMakeReg
symbols.doc: LandlockMakeReg is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_MAKE_REG (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockMakeSock
symbols.doc: LandlockMakeSock is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_MAKE_SOCK (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockMakeSym
symbols.doc: LandlockMakeSym is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_MAKE_SYM (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockReadDir
symbols.doc: LandlockReadDir is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_READ_DIR (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockReadFile
symbols.doc: LandlockReadFile is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_READ_FILE (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockRefer
symbols.doc: LandlockRefer is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_REFER (ABI 2, Linux 5.19).

symbols.name: LandlockRemoveDir
symbols.doc: LandlockRemoveDir is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_REMOVE_DIR (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockRemoveFile
symbols.doc: LandlockRemoveFile is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_REMOVE_FILE (ABI 1).

symbols.name: LandlockRule
symbols.doc:
LandlockRule grants rights beneath a path. It is an alias of the core port's
LandlockRuleValue.

symbols.name: LandlockTruncate
symbols.doc: LandlockTruncate is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_TRUNCATE (ABI 3, Linux 6.2).

symbols.name: LandlockWriteFile
symbols.doc: LandlockWriteFile is LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_WRITE_FILE (ABI 1).

symbols.name: Limit
symbols.doc:
Limit is a soft/hard resource-limit pair for setrlimit(2). It is an alias of
the core port's LimitValue.

symbols.name: Module
symbols.doc:
Module is one module of the running binary, with its release, its commit
and its local directory told apart. It is an alias of the service value.

symbols.name: Mount
symbols.doc:
Mount is one mount a sandboxed child makes in its mount namespace. It is an
alias of the core port's MountValue.

symbols.name: MountBind
symbols.doc: MountBind binds Source onto Target, recursively (systemd BindPaths=).

symbols.name: MountKind
symbols.doc: MountKind is what a Mount mounts. It is an alias of the core port type.

symbols.name: MountReadOnly
symbols.doc: MountReadOnly binds Target onto itself and makes it read-only, recursively (systemd ReadOnlyPaths=) — the zero value.

symbols.name: MountTmpfs
symbols.doc: MountTmpfs mounts an empty tmpfs on Target, nosuid and nodev (systemd TemporaryFileSystem=).

symbols.name: MountTmpfsSticky
symbols.doc: MountTmpfsSticky mounts an empty tmpfs on Target, mode 1777 — sticky, writable by all, as /tmp is —, nosuid and nodev (systemd PrivateTmp=).

symbols.name: MustStart
symbols.doc:
MustStart is like [Start] but panics with the typed error when the spawn fails
— UnsupportedPlatform off Unix/Windows, InvalidSpec, RlimitFailed, … It is the
idiomatic Go MustX opt-in (like [regexp.MustCompile]) for a consumer that
chooses crash-on-failure at its own startup; the SDK itself never panics, and
[Start] is the non-panicking form for normal use. The panic value is the typed
error, so a top-level recover() can classify it via errs.CodeOf / HasCode.

symbols.name: Namespace
symbols.doc:
Namespace is a set of Linux namespaces (Sandbox.Namespaces). It is an alias of
the core port type.

symbols.name: NamespaceCgroup
symbols.doc:
NamespaceCgroup puts the child in a new cgroup namespace (CLONE_NEWCGROUP),
rooted at the group it runs in, Spec.CgroupPath's when one is set — unshared
once the child is placed there.

symbols.name: NamespaceIPC
symbols.doc: NamespaceIPC clones the child into a new IPC namespace (CLONE_NEWIPC).

symbols.name: NamespaceMount
symbols.doc: NamespaceMount gives the child a private copy of the mount namespace (CLONE_NEWNS).

symbols.name: NamespaceNet
symbols.doc: NamespaceNet clones the child into a new network namespace, with a loopback only (CLONE_NEWNET).

symbols.name: NamespacePID
symbols.doc: NamespacePID clones the child into a new PID namespace, as its PID 1 (CLONE_NEWPID).

symbols.name: NamespaceTime
symbols.doc: NamespaceTime clones the child into a new time namespace (CLONE_NEWTIME, Linux 5.6).

symbols.name: NamespaceUTS
symbols.doc: NamespaceUTS clones the child into a new UTS namespace (CLONE_NEWUTS).

symbols.name: NamespaceUser
symbols.doc: NamespaceUser clones the child into a new user namespace (CLONE_NEWUSER).

symbols.name: Open
symbols.doc:
Open returns a handle on a process this one did not spawn, held through a
kernel handle (a pidfd on Linux, a process HANDLE on Windows) so that no
signal reaches another process that reuses the pid. Its Wait is refused with
WaitFailed — only a parent collects an exit status — and every other platform
returns UnsupportedPlatform.

symbols.name: PIDFileRefused

code.public: The PID file cannot be read safely

symbols.doc:
PIDFileRefused is returned by AttachPIDFile for a PID file it cannot read
safely: relative, a symbolic link, not regular, or not one PID.

symbols.name: PTYSize
symbols.doc:
PTYSize is a pseudo-terminal's window size in character cells. It is an alias
of the core port's PTYValue.

symbols.name: ParseBuild
symbols.doc:
ParseBuild describes a BuildInfo from elsewhere — one a test builds by
hand, or debug.ParseBuildInfo's reading of another binary — exactly as
Build describes the running one.

symbols.name: Process
symbols.doc:
Process is the handle to a spawned process: PID, Wait, Signal, SignalGroup,
and a group-aware Stop. It is an alias of the core port interface.

symbols.name: ProcessHandle
symbols.doc:
ProcessHandle is the sibling of Process that reaches the process through a
kernel handle rather than its pid (Handle, SignalHandle). It is an alias of
the core port.

symbols.name: ReadIdentity
symbols.doc:
ReadIdentity reads what the kernel says the running process is. It never
fails: a fact the platform does not give is zero. It hashes the binary:
call it once.

symbols.name: ReservedEnv

code.public: The environment names a variable reserved by the SDK

symbols.doc:
ReservedEnv is returned by Start and Run, before any fork, when Spec.Env names
a key that begins __KITSUNIUM_SDK_PROC_, in any case: the SDK's own spawn
protocol, which such a key would override. errors.Is matches it.

symbols.name: Resource
symbols.doc:
Resource identifies a per-process resource governed by setrlimit(2). It is an
alias of the core port type.

symbols.name: ResourceAS
symbols.doc: ResourceAS limits the process virtual address-space size (RLIMIT_AS).

symbols.name: ResourceCPU
symbols.doc: ResourceCPU limits CPU time in seconds (RLIMIT_CPU).

symbols.name: ResourceCore
symbols.doc: ResourceCore limits the size of a core dump in bytes (RLIMIT_CORE).

symbols.name: ResourceNoFile
symbols.doc: ResourceNoFile limits the highest open file descriptor (RLIMIT_NOFILE).

symbols.name: Result
symbols.doc:
Result is what Run returns: the exit and the head of each output stream. It
is an alias of the core port's ResultValue.

symbols.name: Run
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, spec Spec, opts RunOptions) (result Result, err error)
symbols.canonical: func(ctx context.Context, spec github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/process.Spec, opts github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/process.RunOptions) (result github.com/kitsunium/sdk/pkg/v1/proc/process.Result, err error)
symbols.doc:
Run starts spec, waits for it, and returns its exit with the first
opts.MaxOutputBytes bytes of each output stream, however much the child
writes: the rest is read and discarded, so the child never blocks on a full
pipe. When ctx ends first the child is stopped (SIGTERM, opts.Grace, SIGKILL)
and Run returns what it had with ctx's error. A MaxOutputBytes that is not
positive is refused with InvalidSpec.

symbols.name: RunOptions
symbols.doc:
RunOptions configures Run: the bytes kept from each output stream and the
grace a cancelled run's child is given. It is an alias of the core port's
RunValue.

symbols.name: SIGHUP
symbols.doc: SIGHUP is the hang-up / reload signal many daemons treat as "reconfigure".

symbols.name: SIGINT
symbols.doc: SIGINT is the interrupt signal (Ctrl-C analogue).

symbols.name: SIGKILL
symbols.doc: SIGKILL is the unignorable kill Stop escalates to after the grace window.

symbols.name: SIGQUIT
symbols.doc: SIGQUIT is the quit-with-core signal.

symbols.name: SIGTERM
symbols.doc: SIGTERM is the polite termination request — the default Stop signal.

symbols.name: Sandbox
symbols.doc:
Sandbox is the isolation a child is spawned under (Spec.Sandbox): namespaces,
mounts, a new root, capabilities, no_new_privs, Landlock and seccomp. It is an
alias of the core port's SandboxValue.

symbols.name: SandboxFailed
symbols.doc:
SandboxFailed is returned by Start when a step of Spec.Sandbox failed in the
child before its program ran; the step and errno fields say which and why.

symbols.name: SandboxUnavailable

code.public: The kernel cannot apply the requested confinement

symbols.name: SchedBatch
symbols.doc: SchedBatch is the policy for CPU-bound batch work (SCHED_BATCH).

symbols.name: SchedFIFO
symbols.doc: SchedFIFO is the first-in first-out realtime policy (SCHED_FIFO).

symbols.name: SchedIdle
symbols.doc: SchedIdle runs the child only when nothing else wants the CPU (SCHED_IDLE).

symbols.name: SchedOther
symbols.doc: SchedOther is the normal time-sharing policy (SCHED_OTHER) — the zero value.

symbols.name: SchedPolicy
symbols.doc: SchedPolicy is a CPU scheduling policy. It is an alias of the core port type.

symbols.name: SchedRR
symbols.doc: SchedRR is the round-robin realtime policy (SCHED_RR).

symbols.name: Scheduling
symbols.doc:
Scheduling is the CPU scheduling policy and I/O priority of Spec.Scheduling.
It is an alias of the core port's SchedulingValue.

symbols.name: Seccomp
symbols.doc:
Seccomp is a sandboxed child's system call filter. It is an alias of the core
port's SeccompValue.

symbols.name: SeccompAction
symbols.doc:
SeccompAction is what a seccomp filter does with a call. It is an alias of the
core port type.

symbols.name: SeccompAllow
symbols.doc: SeccompAllow lets the call through (SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW).

symbols.name: SeccompErrno
symbols.doc: SeccompErrno fails the call with SeccompValue.Errno (SECCOMP_RET_ERRNO).

symbols.name: SeccompKill
symbols.doc: SeccompKill kills the whole process (SECCOMP_RET_KILL_PROCESS, Linux 4.14) — the zero value.

symbols.name: Self
symbols.doc:
Self takes a snapshot of the running process. It never fails: a figure the
platform cannot give is zero, and Stats.CPUEstimated says when CPUTime is
the runtime's estimate rather than the kernel's count.

symbols.name: SetOOMScoreAdj
symbols.doc:
SetOOMScoreAdj sets the running process's own OOM-killer bias
(/proc/self/oom_score_adj, -1000 to 1000), so a supervisor can outlive its
children; lowering it needs CAP_SYS_RESOURCE. RlimitFailed when refused,
UnsupportedPlatform off Linux.

symbols.name: Setting
symbols.doc:
Setting is one build setting as the toolchain recorded it, key and value.
It is an alias of the service value.

symbols.name: Signal
symbols.doc:
Signal is a typed, platform-portable OS signal. It is an alias of the core
port type, so process.SIGTERM and a signal parsed elsewhere compare equal.

symbols.name: Spec
symbols.doc:
Spec is the immutable description of a process to spawn — executable,
environment, credentials, isolation topology, and scheduling attributes. It is
an alias of the core port type.

symbols.name: Start
symbols.spelled: func(ctx context.Context, spec Spec) (proc Process, err error)
symbols.doc:
Start spawns the process described by spec and returns a live Process handle.
It delegates to internal/service/proc/exec; ctx is honoured up to the
fork/exec boundary. A bare Spec.Path is searched in the child's PATH (see
the package documentation). On Windows the Unix-only Spec fields are refused
with UnsupportedPlatform; on platforms that are neither Unix nor Windows,
Start itself returns UnsupportedPlatform.

symbols.name: StartSource
symbols.doc: StartSource says where Identity.StartedAt came from. It aliases the service type.

symbols.name: StartSourceInit
symbols.doc: StartSourceInit is the package's initialisation, not the kernel's word.

symbols.name: StartSourceKernel
symbols.doc: StartSourceKernel is the kernel's record of when it started the process.

symbols.name: Stats
symbols.doc:
Stats is the running process at one instant: identity, scheduler settings,
goroutines, heap, collections with their pause distribution, scheduling
latency, and CPU time. Every count is cumulative since the process started.
It is an alias of the service value.

symbols.name: StatusUnknown

code.public: The process ended with an unknown status

symbols.doc:
StatusUnknown is what an attached process's Wait returns once it has ended:
its exit status is not this process's to read.

symbols.name: StdioCapture
symbols.doc:
StdioCapture connects the child to Spec.Stdout/Stderr (io.Writer) and
Spec.Stdin (io.Reader); a nil stream falls back to the null device for that
one stream. The systemd analogue is StandardOutput=/StandardError=/StandardInput=.

symbols.name: StdioInherit
symbols.doc:
StdioInherit shares the parent's stdin/stdout/stderr with the child — the
default and the only behaviour before per-process wiring existed.

symbols.name: StdioMode
symbols.doc:
StdioMode selects how a spawned child's standard streams (stdin, stdout,
stderr) are wired. It is an alias of the core port type; set it on Spec.Stdio.
The zero value is StdioInherit.

symbols.name: StdioNull
symbols.doc:
StdioNull connects every stream to the null device: output is discarded and
the child's stdin returns EOF immediately.

symbols.name: StdioPTY
symbols.doc:
StdioPTY gives the child one pseudo-terminal for stdin, stdout and stderr, as
its controlling terminal in a new session; the master is Terminal.TTY. Linux,
darwin, FreeBSD and OpenBSD.

symbols.name: Terminal
symbols.doc:
Terminal is the sibling of Process for a child started with StdioPTY: TTY,
Resize and Size. It is an alias of the core port.

symbols.name: Toolchain
symbols.doc:
Toolchain is how the toolchain built the binary: its target, compiler,
flags and cgo setting. It is an alias of the service value.

symbols.name: Usage
symbols.doc:
Usage is the page-fault, block-I/O and context-switch accounting an
ExitResult carries beside CPU time and peak RSS, by value, its Known false
where the platform does not supply it. It is an alias of the core port's
UsageValue.

symbols.name: ExitEvent
symbols.doc:
ExitEvent is one child a sweep collected — its pid, its exit and whether a
Process owned it. It aliases the service value.

symbols.name: IsPID1
symbols.doc:
IsPID1 reports whether the current process is the init process (pid 1). It is
false on platforms where the convention does not apply.

symbols.name: New
symbols.doc:
New returns a [Reaper] configured by opts. On Unix it is a SIGCHLD-driven
waitpid loop; elsewhere it is a no-op. The reaper starts idle — call Start.

symbols.name: Option
symbols.doc:
Option configures a [Reaper] returned by [New]. It is an alias of the service
option type so callers compose options without importing internal packages.

symbols.name: ReapFailed
symbols.doc:
ReapFailed is returned by a sweep when wait4 fails with an error other
than the benign ECHILD ("no children") condition.

symbols.name: Reaper
symbols.doc:
Reaper collects terminated child processes so they do not linger as zombies —
the core duty of any PID1 or subreaper. It is an alias of the core port; the
concrete value is platform-selected by [New].

symbols.name: SetChildSubreaper
symbols.doc:
SetChildSubreaper marks the calling process as a child subreaper so orphaned
descendants reparent to it rather than to PID1. It returns [SubreaperFailed]
on a prctl error and [UnsupportedPlatform] off Unix.

symbols.name: SubreaperFailed
symbols.doc:
SubreaperFailed is returned by [SetChildSubreaper] when
prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) fails to arm subreaper mode.

symbols.name: UnsupportedPlatform

code.public: This operation is not supported on this platform

symbols.doc:
UnsupportedPlatform is returned by [SetChildSubreaper] on platforms
without a prctl(PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER) equivalent (e.g. Windows).

symbols.name: WithOnExit
symbols.doc:
WithOnExit registers fn as an observer of every child a sweep collects, an
orphan included: the one record of how a re-parented descendant ended. fn
runs under the sweep lock and must not block; nothing is stored.

symbols.name: WithOnReap
symbols.doc:
WithOnReap registers fn as a post-sweep observer receiving the number of
children reaped in each sweep (including zero). fn must not block. On illumos
and Solaris the loop also sweeps once a second, so there an idle reaper calls
fn with zero once a second.

symbols.name: Apply
symbols.doc:
Apply sets the soft/hard ceilings in limits on the process identified by pid.
A pid of 0 targets the calling process; any other pid targets that process via
prlimit64(2) and needs CAP_SYS_RESOURCE. It returns UnknownResource for an
unmapped resource, RlimitFailed on a syscall failure, and UnsupportedPlatform
off Linux.

symbols.name: Get
symbols.doc:
Get reads the soft/hard ceiling of r for pid (0 is the caller): getrlimit for
the caller, prlimit64 for another pid on Linux, UnsupportedPlatform for
another pid elsewhere.

symbols.name: KeepRaisedNoFile
symbols.doc:
KeepRaisedNoFile makes every child this process spawns from now on inherit
its raised open-file soft limit, instead of the original one the Go runtime
puts back in each child it forks, and returns the limit in force. It acts once
per process. It returns RlimitFailed on a syscall failure and
UnsupportedPlatform off Unix.

symbols.name: Limit
symbols.doc:
Limit is an immutable soft/hard setrlimit(2) pair. It aliases the core proc
LimitValue type.

symbols.name: LimitInfinity
symbols.doc: LimitInfinity is the soft/hard value meaning "no limit" (RLIM_INFINITY).

symbols.name: OpenFiles
symbols.doc:
OpenFiles counts the caller's open descriptors (HANDLES on Windows), to watch
against Get(0, ResourceNoFile). UnsupportedPlatform on OpenBSD, NetBSD and
DragonFly.

symbols.name: PrepareSysProcAttr
symbols.doc:
PrepareSysProcAttr validates limits without issuing any syscall and reports
whether they can be applied on this platform, returning the same typed errors
Apply would (UnknownResource / UnsupportedPlatform). Use it to fail fast at
Spec-construction time; Go's SysProcAttr has no rlimit field, so the actual
application happens post-fork via Apply.

symbols.name: Resource
symbols.doc:
Resource is the abstract, platform-portable resource enum mapped to a
RLIMIT_* constant by the service layer. It aliases the core proc type.

symbols.name: ResourceAS
symbols.doc: ResourceAS limits the process virtual address-space size (RLIMIT_AS).

symbols.name: ResourceCPU
symbols.doc: ResourceCPU limits CPU time in seconds (RLIMIT_CPU).

symbols.name: ResourceCore
symbols.doc: ResourceCore limits the core-dump size in bytes (RLIMIT_CORE).

symbols.name: ResourceData
symbols.doc: ResourceData limits the process data-segment size (RLIMIT_DATA).

symbols.name: ResourceFSize
symbols.doc: ResourceFSize limits the largest file the process may create (RLIMIT_FSIZE).

symbols.name: ResourceMemLock
symbols.doc: ResourceMemLock limits bytes that may be locked into RAM (RLIMIT_MEMLOCK).

symbols.name: ResourceNProc
symbols.doc: ResourceNProc limits the number of processes for the real uid (RLIMIT_NPROC).

symbols.name: ResourceNoFile
symbols.doc:
ResourceNoFile limits the highest open file descriptor (RLIMIT_NOFILE). It
re-exports the core enum value so consumers qualify it as rlimit.ResourceNoFile.

symbols.name: ResourceStack
symbols.doc: ResourceStack limits the process stack size (RLIMIT_STACK).

symbols.name: AttachScope
symbols.doc:
AttachScope bounds the process an untrustworthy PID file may name: a cgroup
v2 subtree and the users it may run as. It is the same type as
proc/process's AttachScope, an alias of the core port's AttachValue.

symbols.name: Attacher
symbols.doc: Attacher adopts a process the engine did not start: MAINPID=, PIDFile=.

symbols.name: BindPath
symbols.doc: BindPath is one entry of BindPaths= or BindReadOnlyPaths=.

symbols.name: BusWatcher
symbols.doc:
BusWatcher follows who owns a Type=dbus unit's BusName=; pkg/v1/proc/dbus's
Conn is one.

symbols.name: CgroupKill
symbols.doc:
CgroupKill is the unit's control group: who belongs to it, and every
process of it signalled at once.

symbols.name: CgroupMembers
symbols.doc:
CgroupMembers is the sibling of CgroupKill a control group that lists its
processes offers: a Type=forking unit guesses its main process among them.

symbols.name: CgroupUnit
symbols.doc:
CgroupUnit is the sibling of CgroupKill a unit's control group offers
when it runs the cgroup modes — KillMode=control-group and mixed,
ExitType=cgroup, Delegate=, OOMPolicy=; proc/cgroup's Linux group is one.

symbols.name: Clock
symbols.doc:
Clock is what every wait of a unit runs on: pkg/v1/clock's System and
ManualClock are clocks here.

symbols.doc:
The codes, for errs.HasCode: a refused configuration (CONFIG_INVALID,
DIRECTIVE_UNSUPPORTED, PRIVILEGE_REFUSED, COMMAND_INVALID) is the caller's to
fix, a job's outcome (START_FAILED, START_LIMIT_HIT, RELOAD_FAILED,
RELOAD_UNSUPPORTED, JOB_CANCELED, UNIT_CLOSED) is the unit's, and
EXIT_UNKNOWN is an adopted process's end.

symbols.name: CodeReloadUnsupported
symbols.doc:
The codes, for errs.HasCode: a refused configuration (CONFIG_INVALID,
DIRECTIVE_UNSUPPORTED, PRIVILEGE_REFUSED, COMMAND_INVALID) is the caller's to
fix, a job's outcome (START_FAILED, START_LIMIT_HIT, RELOAD_FAILED,
RELOAD_UNSUPPORTED, JOB_CANCELED, UNIT_CLOSED) is the unit's, and
EXIT_UNKNOWN is an adopted process's end.

symbols.name: CodeStartFailed
symbols.doc:
The codes, for errs.HasCode: a refused configuration (CONFIG_INVALID,
DIRECTIVE_UNSUPPORTED, PRIVILEGE_REFUSED, COMMAND_INVALID) is the caller's to
fix, a job's outcome (START_FAILED, START_LIMIT_HIT, RELOAD_FAILED,
RELOAD_UNSUPPORTED, JOB_CANCELED, UNIT_CLOSED) is the unit's, and
EXIT_UNKNOWN is an adopted process's end.

symbols.name: CodeStartLimitHit
symbols.doc:
The codes, for errs.HasCode: a refused configuration (CONFIG_INVALID,
DIRECTIVE_UNSUPPORTED, PRIVILEGE_REFUSED, COMMAND_INVALID) is the caller's to
fix, a job's outcome (START_FAILED, START_LIMIT_HIT, RELOAD_FAILED,
RELOAD_UNSUPPORTED, JOB_CANCELED, UNIT_CLOSED) is the unit's, and
EXIT_UNKNOWN is an adopted process's end.

symbols.name: CodeUnitClosed
symbols.doc:
The codes, for errs.HasCode: a refused configuration (CONFIG_INVALID,
DIRECTIVE_UNSUPPORTED, PRIVILEGE_REFUSED, COMMAND_INVALID) is the caller's to
fix, a job's outcome (START_FAILED, START_LIMIT_HIT, RELOAD_FAILED,
RELOAD_UNSUPPORTED, JOB_CANCELED, UNIT_CLOSED) is the unit's, and
